extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of journalism and public opinion; critics and reformers interested in how news is selected and presented
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for what constitutes news, how editors and reporters select and shape items, and the institutional pressures that determine journalistic routines and public information. Focuses on overt acts, record systems, publicity influence, economic constraints, stereotyping, and the limits of daily newsgathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: News requires manifestation/definable shape
rubrics_metrics.description: "There must be a manifestation. The course of events must assume a certain definable shape, and until it is in a phase where some aspect is an accomplished fact, news does not separate itself from the ocean of possible truth.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: going into bankruptcy, a fire, a collision, an assault, a riot, an arrest, a denunciation, the introduction of a bill, a speech, a vote, a meeting, the expressed opinion of a well known citizen, an editorial in a newspaper, a sale, a wage-schedule, a price change, the proposal to build a bridge. The reporter cannot publish vague rumors (libel risk) or private, unobjectified states; something definite must occur that has unmistakable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of news correlates with the system of record
rubrics_metrics.description: "It will be found, I think, that there is a very direct relation between the certainty of news and the system of record.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where good machinery of record exists (stock exchange tickers, election returns, births/deaths/marriages, customs for imports/exports), news can be reported with reliable precision. Topics lacking systematic records (internal trade, over-the-counter transactions, many conditions of industry) yield debatable or neglected news.

rubrics_metrics.name: News is report of what obtrudes, not a mirror of social conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the first instance, therefore, the news is not a mirror of social conditions, but the report of an aspect that has obtruded itself.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News tells when an aspect 'breaks the surface' rather than the slow germination of conditions. Thus much important social reality remains unreported until an overt act or record makes it noticeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine, standardization and stereotypes drive newsgathering
rubrics_metrics.description: "Reporters are not clairvoyant... the range of subjects these comparatively few men manage to cover would be a miracle indeed, if it were not a standardized routine..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardization economizes time, fits page constraints, and gives readers familiar footholds. Stereotypes (labels like 'combine' vs 'group of leading business men') cue readers' reactions and make distant facts comprehensible quickly. Without these conventions the daily press could not operate under deadlines and space limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic pressures and audience interest determine selection and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: "His enterprises depend upon indirect taxation levied by his advertisers upon his readers... In order to secure that circulation, he cannot rely wholly upon news of the greater environment..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors choose items and emphasis according to what will attract or retain readers (and thus advertisers). Competition measured in minutes, page size, libel risk, and the need to interest readers quickly push editors toward indisputable facts and treatments adapted to presumed public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting (newsgathering) is under-resourced and undervalued
rubrics_metrics.description: "Reporting... is the most poorly paid branch of newspaper work, and is the least regarded... able men go into it only by necessity or for experience..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because straight reporting pays poorly and lacks corporate traditions, it attracts fewer trained professionals and less institutional pride, which limits investigative depth and the development of standards that would raise journalistic practice closer to professions like medicine or law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agents/publicity men shape and filter news
rubrics_metrics.description: "The publicity man... presents him a clear picture of a situation out of which he might otherwise make neither head nor tail... He is censor and propagandist, responsible only to his employers..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicity agents act as intermediaries between organized groups and reporters, often closing direct channels to news. They may manufacture 'stunts' to create newsworthy overt acts. Because reporters depend on such convenient formulations, news is often the employers' picture rather than a detached exposition of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex, latent, or systemic issues are unlikely to be covered without special resources
rubrics_metrics.description: "News which requires so much trouble as that to obtain is beyond the resources of a daily press.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matters requiring investigation, time, money, and space (e.g., comprehensive studies of working conditions like Pittsburgh surveys) are rarely undertaken by daily papers. Without official reports or overt acts, deeper truths (standards of living, motives, discrimination, efficiency) remain debatable or unreported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events not objectively scored are reported as opinion or ignored
rubrics_metrics.description: "The events which are not scored are reported either as personal and conventional opinions, or they are not news.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects that lack objective measurement (states of mind, sincerity, national feeling, future policies, private incomes) produce spasmodic, contestable coverage and are susceptible to partisan framing rather than precise factual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: The editor must make rapid, consequential judgments under constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every bulletin requires a swift but complicated judgment... It must be understood, put in relation to other bulletins..., and played up or played down according to its probable interest... The final page is of a definite size, must be ready at a precise moment..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical constraints—deadlines, page/column limits, headline space, libel exposure—force editors to prioritize, standardize, and sometimes disregard subtlety to produce a deliverable newspaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic models diffuse across the press and can institutionalize forms
rubrics_metrics.description: "The way that news was presented became a model for the whole press... It came from the English press... London was the cable and news center..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When certain outlets (e.g., those with cable access) set reporting forms, other papers copy those techniques. Limited access and language barriers can centralize formulation of foreign news in distant centers and allow censors/propagandists to shape stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader identification and inability to rest in the negative produce partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: "In order that he shall enter he must find a familiar foothold... The more passionately involved he becomes, the more he will tend to resent not only a different view... many a newspaper finds that, having honestly evoked the partisanship of its readers, it can not easily... change position."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News is packaged to permit readers to enter and identify with stories; this engagement makes readers adopt positions and resists later editorial reversals. Editors therefore often avoid abrupt changes, preferring to let coverage taper off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good reporters anticipate news before overt acts; skill matters
rubrics_metrics.description: "Naturally there is room for wide difference of opinion as to when events have a shape that can be reported. A good journalist will find news oftener than a hack..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced reporters can recognize precursors (dangerous list of a building, inquiries about climates implying appointment) and thus 'discover' news earlier than others. Such skill partially mitigates the routine limitations but is rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers are ill-suited as substitutes for legal/arbitral procedures in trying disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: "To try disputes by an appeal through the newspapers puts a burden upon newspapers and readers which they cannot and ought not to carry.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because newspapers lack independent filtering of facts and the procedures of law/order, using the press to decide industrial or complex public disputes tends to produce coverage focused on overt incidents and reader inconvenience rather than the substantive issues at stake.
